title: Compute types and virtual machine options
learningObjective: Compare VMs, containers and functions, and describe Azure Virtual Machines, Virtual Machine Scale Sets, availability sets and Azure Virtual Desktop.
foundation: Virtual machines: a whole computer in the cloud with its own OS. Most control, you manage the OS.
Containers: a lightweight package of an app and its dependencies that shares the host's OS kernel. Start in seconds, run the same everywhere.
Functions: small pieces of code that run in response to an event (serverless). No servers to think about; billed per execution.

VM options: one VM; an availability set (VMs spread across racks); a Virtual Machine Scale Set (identical VMs that scale automatically); Azure Virtual Desktop (cloud-hosted Windows desktops for users).
engineer: Compare: VMs virtualise hardware (full OS each, minutes to start, total control). Containers virtualise the OS (share kernel, seconds to start, portable). Functions abstract everything but your code (event-driven, scale to zero on consumption plans).

Azure container options: Azure Container Instances (single containers, fastest start), Azure Container Apps (serverless microservices), Azure Kubernetes Service (orchestration at scale). Docker is the common container format.

Azure Virtual Machines: choose image, size, disks and networking. Use cases: test and development, running applications in the cloud, extending your datacenter, disaster recovery, lift-and-shift migration.

Availability sets: group VMs across fault domains (separate power/network racks, up to 3) and update domains (rebooted at different times during planned maintenance, up to 20). No extra cost; you pay for the VMs. Protects within one datacenter.

Virtual Machine Scale Sets: create and manage a group of identical, load-balanced VMs; scale automatically on demand or schedule; can span availability zones. Ideal for compute, big-data and container workloads.

Azure Virtual Desktop: desktop and app virtualisation in Azure; centralised security with Microsoft Entra ID and MFA; data stays off user devices; multi-session Windows 10/11 Enterprise lets many users share one VM.

animation.caption: Pick compute types for each requirement, then the right VM availability or scale option.

example.title: An e-commerce platform
body: The legacy ERP runs on two VMs in an availability set. The shop front end runs on a scale set across zones that grows from 4 to 20 VMs on Black Friday.
Order emails are sent by an Azure Function, the recommendation service runs in containers on Container Apps, and call-centre staff use Azure Virtual Desktop.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription (a free account works)
permissions: Reader to explore; Contributor to create resources
portal: Create a resource > Virtual machine: Availability options.
Create a resource > Virtual machine scale set: scaling and orchestration.
configuration.cli:
az vm availability-set create -g <rg> -n avset1 --platform-fault-domain-count 2 --platform-update-domain-count 5
az vmss create -g <rg> -n vmss1 --image Ubuntu2404 --instance-count 2 --zones 1 2 3 --generate-ssh-keys

troubleshooting.symptom: Both VMs rebooted at the same time during maintenance.
troubleshooting.cause: They aren't in an availability set or zones.
troubleshooting.fix: Use an availability set (update domains) or zones.

troubleshooting.symptom: Scale set doesn't add VMs under load.
troubleshooting.cause: No autoscale rule, or maximum reached.

comparisons.difference: Containers are lighter and faster but share the host kernel; VMs isolate a full OS.
Scale sets manage identical VMs and autoscale; availability sets only spread VMs across racks.

misconceptions.myth: Containers include a full operating system.
Availability sets protect against datacenter failure.
Azure Virtual Desktop needs one VM per user.

architectureDecisions: Use functions for short, event-driven work.
Use scale sets across zones for scalable, resilient VM workloads.
